one_liner: Zero-dependency Rust crypto crate whose SIMD/asm SHA-2, SHA-3, BLAKE2 and AEADs beat RustCrypto, ring and aws-lc-rs in its benchmarks.
what_it_does: rscrypto is a single pure-Rust crate with no C/FFI and no default dependencies. It covers checksums, SHA-2/SHA-3/SHAKE/BLAKE2/BLAKE3/Ascon hashes, MACs/KDFs, password hashing, signatures, key exchange and seven AEADs (AES-GCM, AES-GCM-SIV, AES-SIV, ChaCha20-Poly1305, XChaCha20-Poly1305, AEGIS-256, Ascon-AEAD128), each behind its own Cargo feature. Hashes implement the crate's own `Digest` trait: one-shot `Sha256::digest(data)` or streaming `new`/`update`/`finalize`, where `finalize(&self)` returns a fixed array. AEADs take typed keys and nonces and offer combined, detached and `alloc` Vec helpers. It is a primitives crate, not a TLS stack, and it does not implement RustCrypto's `digest`/`aead` traits.
how_it_is_fast: Three-tier dispatch (compile-time target features, then cached runtime CPU detection, then portable Rust) routes each primitive to a per-ISA kernel. SHA-256 uses the Intel SHA extensions (SHA-NI) or the ARMv8 SHA2 instructions; SHA-512 uses AVX2/AVX-512VL kernels based on the Gueron-Krasnov two-block schedule; on s390x the IBM Z CPACF KIMD instruction runs SHA-2 and absorbs SHA-3 blocks in hardware. Single-message SHA-3 on x86-64 and AArch64 is portable Keccak-f[1600] using XKCP's 'Bebigokimisa' lane-complementing trick; the AVX-512 and ARM SHA3 kernels only serve two-state paired paths. On AEADs, Linux x86-64 gets in-house VAES-512 AES-GCM and GCM-SIV assembly (16-, 64- and 128-block variants) plus ChaCha20-Poly1305 assembly adapted from AWS-LC/BoringSSL, and BLAKE2 gets AVX2/AVX-512VL row-vectorized compression.
when_to_use: You want one dependency-free, no_std-capable Rust crate for SHA-2, SHA-3, BLAKE2 and AEADs instead of mixing RustCrypto, ring and aws-lc-rs, and you can live with a pre-1.0 API.
SHA-3/SHAKE-heavy workloads: the fastest-external geomean is 2.27-2.38x over RustCrypto sha3, with zero losses in 88-104 rows per variant.
AES-GCM-SIV or AES-GCM on AVX-512/VAES x86-64 Linux: geomeans of 2.20x/2.34x (GCM-SIV) and 1.80x/1.83x (GCM) against the fastest of RustCrypto, ring and aws-lc-rs.
Mixed-ISA fleets that include IBM z16 (s390x) or POWER10, where it ships native kernels and posts its widest margins (2.77x per-host geomean on s390x).
Pure-Rust XChaCha20-Poly1305: 173 wins, 3 ties and 0 losses, a 1.43x geomean against RustCrypto (the only competitor benchmarked for it).
when_not_to_use: You need a third-party audit, FIPS 140-3 validation or a whole-crate constant-time guarantee. The README says it has none of these; constant-time claims are per operation and per target in ct.toml.
Your code is generic over RustCrypto's `digest`/`aead` traits or uses ring/aws-lc-rs types. rscrypto has its own traits and no dependencies, so every call site changes.
BLAKE2 or ChaCha20-Poly1305 alone would justify the switch. Their margins are thin (1.07-1.13x geomean, with roughly half the rows ties, e.g. blake2b256 101 wins, 99 ties).
You need a stable, slow-moving dependency. Versions 0.1 to 0.9 shipped in four months (May-Aug 2026), and main already requires Rust 1.100.0 and pins a nightly toolchain.
You would adopt the whole stack for ECDSA. P-256/P-384 loses overall (0.87x fastest-external geomean), and the 2026-08-18 run recorded a severe s390x signing regression.

integration.dependencies: none by default; optional getrandom (OS entropy), rayon (`parallel` BLAKE3/Argon2) and serde
integration.min_toolchain: Published 0.9.0 declares Rust 1.91 on crates.io. The main branch (README says 0.10, not yet published) declares rust-version 1.100.0 and edition 2024, and pins nightly-2026-09-25.
integration.platforms: Portable Rust anywhere. Accelerated and tested on Linux x86-64, AArch64, POWER (ppc64le), IBM Z (s390x) and RISC-V, Windows x86-64, Apple Silicon macOS and wasm32 (simd128). Windows AArch64 is compile-only; x86_64-apple-darwin is unsupported.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented explicitly. Hashers and ciphers are owned values updated through &mut self. CPU detection is cached process-wide on first use, and capability overrides must happen before the first platform::caps() call.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same algorithms and byte-identical outputs, but its own Digest/Aead traits and typed key/nonce API replace RustCrypto's digest/aead traits and the ring/aws-lc-rs interfaces, so call sites must be rewritten.

gotchas: no_std builds select kernels only from compile-time target features. Without -C target-cpu or target-feature flags they run portable Rust (no SHA-NI, VAES and so on). The published scorecard was built with -C target-cpu=native.
The `portable-only` feature only disables runtime detection. It does not remove the compiled SIMD/asm code or override compile-time target features.
Some paths stay portable by design: single-message SHA-3 on x86-64/AArch64 (the vector Keccak kernels are two-state only) and SHA-256 on POWER, where the vector kernel lost to portable Rust.

The 2026-08-18 AEAD rows time buffer restoration (copy-and-encrypt), and the BLAKE2 rows include duplicated cases. The maintainer flags both but has not recomputed those historical ratios. The newer 2026-09-14 run (19,614 cases) has no curated ratios yet.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over blake2b_simd, the official BLAKE3 crate or keccak-batch when you want one dependency-free crate covering SHA-2, SHA-3, BLAKE2/3 and AEADs, with runtime dispatch on x86, ARM, POWER and s390x. Stay with blake2b_simd or official BLAKE3 for a mature single-algorithm crate (rscrypto's BLAKE3 median against official blake3 is only 1.04x), and with hashtree or keccak-batch for batched many-message hashing.
verified_claims_summary: On the 2026-08-18 eight-host Linux snapshot, rscrypto's fastest-external geomean was 1.27-1.30x on SHA-256/384/512 (against RustCrypto sha2, ring and aws-lc-rs), 2.27-2.38x on SHA3 (against RustCrypto sha3) and 1.07-1.13x on BLAKE2 (against RustCrypto blake2 and dryoc). The hosts were Zen4/Zen5, Graviton3/4, Power10, z16, Ice Lake and Sapphire Rapids, running commit 7eb44e9 built with nightly-2026-07-17, target-cpu=native and fat LTO, with Criterion over 0 B-1 MiB inputs. The AEAD geomeans, against RustCrypto, ring, aws-lc-rs and the aegis/ascon-aead crates, were 1.80x/1.83x (AES-128/256-GCM), 2.20x/2.34x (AES-GCM-SIV), 1.12x (ChaCha20-Poly1305), 1.43x (XChaCha20-Poly1305), 1.23x (AEGIS-256) and 1.39x (Ascon-AEAD128). OpenSSL itself was never measured.
status_note: Active single-author project: first release May 2026, 0.9.0 on crates.io in August 2026 (about 1.5k downloads), commits through 2026-09-26. It is MIT OR Apache-2.0 and usable as a crate today, but it is pre-1.0, unaudited and changing fast.
